newsitem.title: GERMANY: BASKETBALL-BASKETBALL BOOMS IN UNIFIED BERLIN.
newsitem.headline: BASKETBALL-BASKETBALL BOOMS IN UNIFIED BERLIN.

text.p: The Berlin Wall has crumbled and Germany has reunited since National Basketball Association (NBA) veteran Detlef Schrempf last played in his native land.
In the meantime, soccer, formerly unchallenged in the German capital, no longer enjoys the undivided attention of the sporting public.
Instead, basketball has made an improbable breakthrough into the country's heart, especially in Berlin, a city hungry for a winner and without a single first division soccer team.

Alba Berlin, one of the top basketball teams in the German league and performing with credit in the champions EuroLeague, have jumped into the media void left by the absence of any strong local soccer clubs.
Outdoor "streetball" basketball tournaments in Berlin draw thousands of players each summer for spirited weekends of three-on-three games in front of the Olympic Stadium.

"The last time I played in Germany, a lot of people didn't even know what basketball was," said Schrempf, who led the Seattle Supersonics in a recent exhibition match in Berlin against the Indiana Pacers.

"The excitement over the game in Germany now is tremendous. You see kids wearing NBA T-shirts everywhere. I've never seen a crowd like this for basketball in Germany before. I just hope it keeps growing."

Three factors have fuelled the sport's surge -- Schrempf's heroics in the NBA, which are closely followed in the local sports pages, the popularity of the U.S. "Dream Team" and the German national team's surprise European championship win in 1993.

The NBA, paying tribute to the popularity of the sport in Germany, recently played its first exhibition game in Germany. Tickets were sold out months in advance with 10,000 spectators packing Berlin's Deutschlandhalle arena.

"Germany is the number one market right now in Europe and the growth has been dramatic in the last few years," NBA commissioner David Stern said before the match, referring to sales of NBA merchandise that now exceed $80 million per year.
The NBA has been earning additional unspecified millions from Germany's DSF all-sports television network for showing NBA games.
The German Basketball Federation (DBB) estimates there are more than one million playing the sport -- double the number of just five years ago.
Thousands of outdoor basketball courts have been built in recent years on playgrounds and schoolyards.
"Basketball has become the most popular sport for school children," said DBB spokesman Christoph Winck.
A recent survey that showed 70 percent of schoolchildren wanted basketball included in their gym classes. "That was more than any other sport -- even soccer," said Winck.
Soccer dominates sports pages in many cities but in Berlin extensive basketball coverage stands out in sharp contrast.
Alba Berlin recently moved into a new 8,500-seat arena in formerly communist east Berlin. It has been sold out for most Alba home games this year.
Dietmar Wenck, a sportswriter for Berlin's Der Tagesspiegel newspaper, believes the success of Alba Berlin has helped contribute to the game's popularity.

Alba are top of the German league and undefeated in their first 10 games this season. Two wins from five matches in the EuroLeague, one away against top-rated Greeks Olympiakos, represent an encouraging start at the top level.
Stars include Henning Harnisch, one of the German national team's most profilic scorers, and Henrik Rodl, an ex-college player in the U.S.

The team is coached by Svateslav Pesic, who led Germany to their European championship title in 1993. Sascha Obradovic, who played for Yugoslavia in the Atlanta Olympics, is Alba's sharp-shooting point guard.

"Berlin sports fans are starved for a successful team," Wenck said. "They want a winner and certainly Alba are able to get more media attention in Berlin than they would if there were two first division soccer teams here."
